current_event.title: New hire handbook
current_event.description: Welcome to the product engineering group. Before your career clock starts, this handbook sets out the public rules. Everything in it is part of the published game design, and you can use it for long-term planning.

current_event.description: The team has one place at an industry conference. It is a good trip with plenty of visibility, and word is it will go to you or Jo. The list is due next week.

choices.action: Give Jo fair credit for her strengths and say she would be a good fit

Say you each have strengths, and suggest choosing whoever fits the brief best
Hint at gaps in Jo's recent work

current_event.title: An unpublished restructure, and a friend about to buy a flat
current_event.description: You were copied on a restricted leadership note: a draft Q2 reorganisation. Lynx may be folded into Falcon Recs, with about 15% fewer roles. Nothing has been announced. Over dinner last night your friend and colleague Sienna said she wants to put in an offer on a flat, with the deposit already saved, and asked: “Is your team stable? I’m about to sign.” Her mother is ill and she needs the place.

choices.action: Hint that things may move soon and she should be careful, without naming the document
Say you cannot comment on internal plans or promise that any role is safe, so she must weigh the risk herself
Tell her privately what is planned and ask her to keep it strictly confidential

current_event.title: An unpublished restructure, and a friend about to buy a flat
current_event.description: Sienna holds off signing. Two weeks later the change is announced and she thanks you. Your manager senses a leak and starts checking who knew.

choices.action: Go to your manager and admit you dropped a vague hint
Stay silent

current_event.title: One conference place, and a question about Jo
current_event.description: Your manager nods and says no more. Two days later the list is out: Jo is going. She thanks you in front of the team for 'putting in a word'. A week later she shares client leads from the conference, and your manager praises her in the team channel. You have to decide how you feel about it and what to do next.

choices.action: Congratulate her and ask what she got out of it
Congratulate her in public, then tell your manager privately you want the next one

Monthly base salary: +0.3 (L1)

current_event.title: Going for a valuable certification that takes months
current_event.description: There is a well-regarded certification in the industry that would help your career, but preparing for it would take months of evenings and weekends. The exam fee is not cheap either. You are not sure whether to start now.

choices.action: Set a steady revision plan over several months, broken into daily tasks you can finish
Sign up, then study in fits and starts, and cram at the last minute
Drop the idea because it looks too hard

current_event.title: Lunch with the team, or keep the break to yourself
current_event.description: At noon the team usually heads to a café near the office to swap project gossip and guesses about what your manager is thinking. It is where people pick up the unofficial news. For the past few months you have eaten at your desk or gone for a walk instead. You get a real break and are sharper in the afternoon. Colleagues have started calling you the lone wolf. At last week’s offsite your manager said you should mix with the team a bit more.

choices.action: Switch to lunching with colleagues at least three days a week
Keep skipping the café, and let a strong afternoon prove the point
Compromise: Tuesdays and Thursdays with the team, the break to yourself the rest

current_event.title: The office war over windows and heating
current_event.description: The temperature in your corner of the open-plan office is a running sore. Hugh always feels hot and throws the windows open as soon as he arrives. Maya always feels cold, so she shuts them and turns the radiator up. It can go back and forth several times a day. Today they snap at each other in front of everyone. Nobody else wants to step in, and everyone looks at you: you are fairly neutral, and people listen to you.

choices.action: Propose a middle temperature, plus a small extra for each: a desk fan, a draught screen

Keep your head down and work. It's not your problem

Maya always feels cold, so she shuts them and turns the radiator up. It can go back and forth several times a day. Today they snap at each other in front of everyone. Nobody else wants to step in, and everyone looks at you: you are fairly neutral, and people listen to you.

choices.action: Propose a middle temperature, plus a small extra for each: a desk fan, a draught screen
Make the call: set the temperature most people like, and tell them both to stop
Keep your head down and work. It's not your problem

current_event.title: Forgetting to water the office plants on your rota
current_event.description: Facilities has you on the rota to water the communal plants this week. You got busy and forgot. On Wednesday, Facilities pings you: the plants are almost dead.

choices.action: Water them today and set a calendar reminder
Apologise and ask a colleague to cover this once
Treat it as too small to matter

current_event.title: How blunt to be in a code-review comment
current_event.description: Priya, who has just joined, opens her first merge request. The design is clearly wrong. You can write in the review that this will blow up in production, or you can ask questions until she sees it herself. The team's culture is fairly direct, and HR has just started talking about psychological safety.

choices.action: Name the problem directly and mark it as must-fix
Use questions so she spots the issue herself
Approve it, and explain on Slack afterwards

current_event.title: The office war over windows and heating
current_event.description: You set out what each of them needs and suggest a fixed middle temperature, a small screen to keep the draught off Maya, and a desk fan for Hugh. Both feel looked after, and most of the heat goes out of the row. To make it happen, someone has to ask facilities for the extras.

choices.action: Take the lead with facilities and get the extras in
You had the idea. They can chase it themselves

response.events:
Monthly base salary: +0.3 (L1)

An HR partner you get on with says, smiling, you've been doing all right lately. Keep it up.

current_event.title: Who picks up the bill at a client lunch
current_event.description: You have taken a client out for a work lunch. As it winds down they say, "Let me get this," and make a move for the bill. This is ordinary client entertaining, so your side is meant to pay. How do you handle the moment?

choices.action: Having already paid quietly at the desk, say, "This one's on us. You can host next time"
Wrestle over the bill at the table until it gets awkward
Go along with it and let the client pay

current_event.title: Choosing a stack for a new module
current_event.description: You need to pick a stack for a new module. You could write the team's mature stack in your sleep, and it would almost certainly deliver on time. There is also a more modern framework with an active community that fits better in the long term. But neither you nor the team has used it in production, so expect pitfalls and an uncertain first release. The module is not on the critical path and the timetable is fairly generous. Your manager leaves the decision entirely to you. A proposal is due at next week's architecture huddle.

choices.action: Adopt the new framework and use this low-risk module to build experience
Stick with the mature stack and put reliable delivery first
